title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 59–60
description: Advanced vocabulary for physical space, crowding and layout, informal time idioms, and precise descriptions of duration and timing.

units.title: Unit 59 — Space: no room to swing a cat
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 124–125 (PDF pages 126–127).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish extensive, spacious, roomy and rambling through characteristic contexts and connotations.
Differentiate negative cramped, poky and congested from positive compact and bustling.
Use fixed expressions of crowding and movement, including hemmed in, packed in like sardines and squeeze in.
Apply the uncountable sense of room and collocations such as ample room, make room and take up room.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, adjective tables, examples and Language help note on uncountable room
Exercises 59.1–59.4, including the estate-agent advertisement and register contrasts

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: The campus offers extensive sports facilities spread across several buildings.
items.note: Used of facilities, networks, grounds or areas covering a large range or extent; not simply a synonym of expensive.

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: The renovated library is spacious enough for group discussions and individual study.
items.note: Positive adjective for a place with plenty of room; appropriate in property descriptions.

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: We chose a roomy car so that four adults could travel comfortably.
items.note: Often describes vehicles, rooms or clothing that offer generous interior space.

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: Their conference centre is a rambling old building with corridors leading in several directions.
items.note: A rambling building spreads over an irregular layout, sometimes inconveniently; not automatically a positive selling point.

items.pt: grandes espaços abertos; amplas áreas descampadas
items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: She moved to the countryside because she missed the wide open spaces of her childhood.
items.note: Fixed expression for broad, unobstructed landscapes, often with few buildings.

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: Small research stations are scattered across the region rather than concentrated in one city.
items.note: Scattered suggests distribution in separate, sometimes irregular positions; often followed by across or over.

items.pt: espalhado; distribuído por uma área extensa
items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: The university departments are spread out, so students frequently need to travel between buildings.
items.note: Describes buildings or people separated across an area instead of clustered together.

items.pt: espaço de sobra; espaço mais do que suficiente
items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: There is ample room for the new equipment beside the test bench.
items.note: Ample means more than enough; room here is an uncountable noun meaning space.

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: Could you make room for one more chair at the table?
items.note: Room is uncountable in the sense of available space; make room for somebody or something.

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: The packaging takes up too much room in the storage cupboard.
items.note: Take up room or space means occupy available capacity; room is uncountable here.

items.section: A · Occupying a lot of space
items.example: We still have plenty of room on the shelf for another set of books.
items.note: There is plenty of room, not plenty of rooms, when referring to space rather than separate rooms.

items.example: The technicians struggled to work safely in the cramped control room.
items.note: Negative adjective stressing discomfort caused by limited space; more neutral in register than poky.

items.example: The guesthouse offered a poky little room with barely enough space for a suitcase.
items.note: Informal and negative; typically describes a very small room or flat.

items.pt: congestionado; lotado por tráfego ou pessoas
items.example: The main streets became congested after several roads were closed.
items.note: Often used for roads, urban areas or waterways full of traffic; negative unlike bustling.

items.example: The student chose a compact camera that fitted easily into her jacket pocket.
items.note: Often positive: small but conveniently designed; unlike cramped or poky, does not imply discomfort.

items.pt: cercado; sem espaço para se mover
items.example: We were hemmed in by parked vehicles and could not leave the car park.
items.note: Usually be hemmed in by something, meaning surrounded so that movement is restricted.

items.example: The hotel stands beside a bustling market full of cafes and small shops.
items.note: Suggests lively, energetic activity; generally more positive than congested or crowded.

items.word: not enough room to swing a cat
items.pt: espaço tão pequeno que mal dá para se mexer
items.example: There is not enough room to swing a cat in the tiny kitchen.
items.note: Informal idiom emphasising very little space; not about an actual animal.

items.example: We were packed in like sardines on the commuter train.
items.note: Informal simile for severe overcrowding; usually describes people.

items.example: The corridors form a labyrinth that visitors find difficult to navigate.
items.note: Can literally be a maze or describe a confusing arrangement of passages or rooms.

items.example: A stone wall marks the boundary between the two properties.
items.note: The dividing line at the edge of an area; often mark the boundary.

items.pt: ampliação; parte acrescentada a uma construção
items.example: The family built an extension at the back of the house to create a larger kitchen.
items.note: In property contexts, an added part of a building that increases usable space.

items.pt: na parte de trás; nos fundos
items.example: The deliveries entrance is at the rear of the building.
items.note: At the rear is a slightly more formal way of saying at the back.

items.example: The organisers tried to cram twenty participants into a room designed for twelve.
items.note: Cram something or people into a restricted space stresses excessive or forceful packing.

items.pt: encaixar-se; conseguir entrar em um espaço apertado
items.example: Although the lift was almost full, she managed to squeeze in.
items.note: Fit into a very limited remaining space; may be used without an object.

items.pt: um aperto; situação em que as pessoas ficam espremidas
items.example: With everyone invited, the celebration could be a bit of a squash.
items.note: Informal British expression for too many people sharing a small space.

items.pt: enfiar em; colocar apressadamente dentro de
items.example: He stuffed the documents into his bag before catching the train.
items.note: Stuff something into a place suggests pushing it in quickly, often without much care.

items.example: After the storm, loose papers were scattered all over the courtyard.
items.note: Describes separate objects distributed irregularly, often followed by across, around or all over.

units.title: Unit 60 — Time: once in a blue moon
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 126–127 (PDF pages 128–129).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Time · idioms, duration and temporal register
learningObjectives: Use informal time idioms appropriately, distinguishing permanence, short notice, rarity and last-minute timing.
Choose precise advanced adjectives for brief, extended, repeated, incipient and inexorable phenomena.
Recognise typical collocations such as fleeting glimpse, protracted negotiations and inexorable advance of time.
Use simultaneous, duration, prolong and repeatedly in formal descriptive contexts.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, idiom meanings and adjective-collocation table
Exercises 60.1–60.4 and relevant collocation and grammar contrasts

items.pt: muito raramente; de vez em quando, mas quase nunca
items.example: These old friends live far apart and meet only once in a blue moon.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning very infrequently, not necessarily once a month.

items.pt: em toda a minha vida; desde que me entendo por gente
items.example: In all my born days, I have never seen such an unusual building.
items.note: Informal and rather old-fashioned: all one's born days means throughout one's life.

items.example: I'll finish this email and join you in a mo.
items.note: Very informal British short form of in a moment; use in casual speech.

items.example: I'll be with you in a sec once I have saved the file.
items.note: Informal shortened form of in a second; it need not mean literally one second.

items.example: I'll check the figures and call you back in a tick.
items.note: Informal British way to say very soon; less common in some varieties of English.

items.example: With the updated software, the team finished the routine checks in less than no time.
items.note: Informal emphatic expression for an extremely short period, not a literal negative duration.

items.example: I'll bring the spare key in a jiffy.
items.note: Informal expression meaning very soon; slightly playful or old-fashioned in some contexts.

items.pt: há muitos e muitos anos; há uma eternidade
items.example: She's been running the village shop for donkey's years.
items.note: Informal British idiom meaning for a very long time; not a precise duration.

items.example: The same family has owned the cottage since the year dot.
items.note: Humorous informal expression meaning since an extremely long time ago.

items.pt: até não acabar mais; por tempo indefinido
items.example: They can debate the proposal till the cows come home without reaching an agreement.
items.note: Informal idiom for an indefinitely long period; until the cows come home is also possible.

items.pt: para ficar para sempre; em definitivo
items.example: He gave his nephew the old bicycle for keeps, not just for the weekend.
items.note: Informal phrase meaning permanently, particularly when giving or keeping something.

items.pt: de uma vez por todas; definitivamente
items.example: After years of commuting, she moved closer to work for good.
items.note: Means permanently rather than temporarily; wider uses than for keeps.

items.pt: bem a tempo; no último instante
items.example: The engineers restored the cooling system in the nick of time to prevent the test from being cancelled.
items.note: Just before it would be too late; suggests a narrowly avoided problem.

items.pt: passado da idade; considerado velho demais para algo
items.example: The actor rejected the suggestion that he was over the hill at fifty.
items.note: Informal and potentially unkind expression implying someone is too old to perform as before.

items.pt: passado da idade; sem a capacidade ou o vigor de antes
items.example: Critics claimed that the veteran athlete was past it, but she still won the race.
items.note: Informal and potentially dismissive; means no longer as capable or successful as before.

items.pt: um ex-famoso; alguém que já teve sucesso, mas caiu no esquecimento
items.example: The singer refused to accept that the press had turned him into a has-been.
items.note: Usually disparaging noun for someone formerly famous or successful but no longer so.

items.pt: num piscar de olhos; muito rapidamente
items.example: Once the access code arrived, she completed the registration in a flash.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning extremely quickly, not specifically soon in the future.

items.example: Once the design was approved, work progressed at a rate of knots.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning very fast; originally refers to speed measured in knots.

items.example: She caught a fleeting glimpse of the bird before it disappeared behind the trees.
items.note: Very brief; commonly a fleeting glimpse, moment, visit or smile.

items.example: The council launched a lengthy investigation into the funding decision.
items.note: Takes a long time; neutral or slightly negative when discussing delays or processes.

items.example: The district has a transient population because many residents stay only for a few months.
items.note: Relatively formal; lasting or staying for only a short period.

items.pt: persistente; contínuo; difícil de fazer cessar
items.example: Persistent complaints eventually prompted the company to review its policy.
items.note: Continues or recurs over time despite attempts to stop it; common with problems or criticism.

items.example: The report examines the inexorable decline of the old industrial district.
items.note: Formal: continuing with seemingly no possibility of being stopped; often with decline, rise or pressure.

items.example: The mediator noticed signs of incipient panic among the waiting passengers.
items.note: Formal: just beginning to emerge; often incipient panic, rage or rebellion.

items.pt: prolongado; que se arrasta por muito tempo
items.example: After protracted negotiations, the two organisations finally reached an agreement.
items.note: Formal: drawn out over an unusually long period, sometimes longer than necessary.

items.example: A lingering scent of freshly brewed coffee filled the hallway.
items.note: Lasts or fades slowly after its source has gone; common with scent, smile or memory.

items.example: She had only a fleeting glimpse of the revised design before the screen changed.
items.note: Characteristic collocation combining a brief act of seeing with very short duration.

items.pt: negociações prolongadas; negociações que se arrastam
items.example: The parties reached a compromise only after protracted negotiations.
items.note: Formal collocation suggesting drawn-out discussions rather than merely detailed ones.

items.example: The novel reflects on the inexorable advance of time and the limits of memory.
items.note: Formal literary collocation suggesting time moves forward regardless of human wishes.

items.pt: simultâneo; que ocorre ao mesmo tempo
items.example: Simultaneous inspections took place at all three manufacturing sites.
items.note: Two or more events happening at the same time; simultaneously is the related adverb.

items.pt: durante todo o período de; pelo tempo que durar
items.example: Visitors must wear protective clothing for the duration of the laboratory tour.
items.note: Duration denotes the whole length of an event; commonly for the duration of something.

items.example: The chair declined to prolong the meeting when the agenda was complete.
items.note: Transitive verb: make an event or process last longer; often with negotiations, treatment or a meeting.

items.pt: com pouca antecedência; em cima da hora
items.example: The technical team managed to organise an additional test at short notice.
items.note: Means there was very little warning or time to prepare; British expression.

items.example: The supplier was repeatedly asked to confirm the delivery date.
items.note: Adverb meaning again and again; a useful alternative to many times.

items.example: The two laboratories simultaneously reported the same unexpected result.
items.note: Adverb corresponding to simultaneous; helpful when describing parallel events.
